content: Moving on is not deleting the person. It is letting your day belong to you again. Eat, sleep, and show up to work in smaller pieces than your pride wants. Grief is physical.
Remove daily triggers you can control: their hoodie on the chair, the chat pinned at the top, the cafe that was only yours together. Keep one memory if you must. Do not keep the museum.
Tell one honest person the unpretty version. Isolation turns heartbreak into identity. New tiny plans — a class, a Sunday walk, a call with a cousin — teach your body that the future exists.
If sadness stays heavy for weeks, or you cannot function, talk to a mental health professional. MyTalk can support the lonely evenings; it does not replace clinical care or emergency help.

title: How to Get Closure When They Will Not Apologise
excerpt: You can finish a chapter without the speech you deserved.
author: Arjun Singh
content: Closure is often imagined as their perfect explanation. Most people who hurt you cannot or will not give that. Waiting for it keeps them in charge of your ending.
Write the conversation you needed, then read it to yourself or to a listener. Name what happened, what it cost, and what you will not repeat. That is closure you can actually finish.
Forgiveness is optional. Understanding is optional. Safety and a next step are not. You can release the daily replay without calling them a good person.
If the story loops at night, say it out loud once in a structured way. A MyTalk session is a place to put the ending down so it stops living only in your head.

title: The No Contact Rule Without Cruelty
excerpt: Space after a breakup is a recovery tool, not a tactic to make them chase.
author: Meera Sharma
content: No contact means you stop texting, calling, and checking for a set period so your nervous system can leave the loop. It is for your clarity. Using silence to punish or bait a response keeps you attached.
Tell them once if a conversation is owed: ‘I need space and I will not be in touch for now.’ Then hold it. Logistics about shared flats or children are exceptions, kept brief and practical.
Expect grief in week two when the habit of reaching is loudest. Plan those hours: walk, shower, food, one safe person. Do not ‘just check’ the profile.
If no contact feels impossible alone, book a listener for the urge itself. MyTalk exists so the hardest hour has somewhere to go that is not their chat window.

title: Orbiting After a Breakup: When They Watch but Will Not Talk
excerpt: Story views and likes with no conversation keep the wound open.
author: MyTalk Editorial
content: Orbiting is staying in your digital sky after the relationship landed. They watch stories, like an old photo, and never actually speak. It feels like contact. It is not care.
You can mute, restrict, or remove them. You do not need a speech. If you share friends, you can stay polite in person and still close the private window.
Ask what you hope the like means. Usually it means they want the feeling of you without the responsibility. You can want them and still refuse that deal.
Healing speeds up when the feed stops flickering with their name. Fill the gap with a real conversation — a friend, or a confidential MyTalk session on the nights the mute button feels cruel.

title: Breadcrumbing: Why Mixed Signals Feel So Addictive
excerpt: Random likes, late ‘you up’ texts, and just enough hope to keep you waiting.
author: Aditya Kulkarni
content: Breadcrumbing is attention without investment. A meme, a midnight voice note, a ‘we should meet’ that never becomes a date. You stay slightly hungry, which is the point.
Your brain treats intermittent rewards like a slot machine. The rare warm message feels bigger than ten consistent ones would. That is biology, not destiny.
Decide what counts as effort: a plan with a day and a place. If they will not offer that, stop replying to crumbs. Silence is a boundary, not a game.
If you keep reopening the chat, tell someone. Accountability beats willpower at 1 a.m. A MyTalk chat can be the place you put the urge before you send ‘you around?’

title: What Is a Situationship? Meaning, Signs, and a Clean Exit
excerpt: Almost together, never defined — and why it exhausts you.
author: Ishita Banerjee
content: A situationship is intimacy without an agreement. You act like a couple in private and like a maybe in public. Plans stay vague. Labels are ‘too much’. Your life bends around their mood.
It feels exciting because uncertainty spikes dopamine. It feels lonely because you cannot introduce them, plan a festival, or ask for care without sounding needy.
Ask once, clearly: ‘Are we building something exclusive, or keeping this casual?’ A real answer is a choice. A joke, a delay, or ‘why ruin it’ is also an answer.
Leaving is allowed even if the good nights were real. Grieve the almost. Then stop auditioning for a title they will not give.

title: Love Bombing vs Real Interest: How to Tell the Difference
excerpt: Intense early attention can be romance — or a setup for control.
author: Arjun Singh
content: Real interest is warm and paced. Love bombing is overwhelming: constant praise, future talk in week one, gifts that feel too large, and irritation when you need a night off.
The test is what happens when you set a limit. A caring person adjusts. A love-bombing pattern punishes the limit, calls you cold, or threatens to withdraw the fantasy.
Speed is not proof of depth. Ask about their last relationship, their friends, and how they handle a no. Watch consistency after the first high.
If you already feel addicted to the attention and scared to slow down, that fear is information. Name it with someone outside the rush before you make a promise.

title: What Gaslighting Sounds Like in Everyday Arguments
excerpt: Phrases that make you doubt your memory — and how to steady yourself.
author: Meera Sharma
content: Gaslighting is not a normal disagreement. It is a pattern of making you distrust what you saw, felt, or remember. ‘That never happened’, ‘you are too sensitive’, and ‘everyone else thinks you are dramatic’ are common lines.
One clumsy sentence is not abuse. The pattern is: you raise a fact, they rewrite it, you apologise for being confused, and the original issue disappears. Over time you stop bringing things up.

Keep a private record of dates and exact words if you feel your memory slipping. Check with one safe person who is not invested in the fight. You are allowed to say, ‘I am not debating whether I felt hurt.’
If you are unsure whether you are overreacting, talk it through somewhere confidential. MyTalk is for sorting reality from fog, not for diagnosing your partner in public.

title: Red Flags on a First Date in India
excerpt: Early warning signs that have nothing to do with astrology compatibility.
author: MyTalk Editorial
content: A first date is a sample, not a verdict on your worth. Still, some samples tell you enough. Insults dressed as jokes, pressure to drink or leave the public place, and contempt for waiters or drivers usually travel home with the person.

Watch how they talk about an ex. Bitterness about ‘all women’ or ‘all men’ is a preview. Watch whether they ask you anything. A monologue about salary, status, or how their mother will judge you is not romance.
In Indian dating, family comments arrive early. Curiosity is fine. An interrogation about caste, income, and ‘character’ on coffee one is a boundary moment. You can smile and still end the evening.
You do not owe a second date to politeness. Tell a friend your live location, and if something felt off, say it to a trusted listener before you talk yourself out of it.

title: Green Flags Worth Keeping: Signs of a Healthy Relationship
excerpt: The quiet behaviours that matter more than chemistry on date three.
author: Aditya Kulkarni
content: Green flags are boring in the best way. They reply when they said they would. They remember the small story. They can disagree without humiliation. They introduce you to friends without a performance.

Look for repair. Everyone snaps. A healthy person comes back, owns the tone, and tries again. Look for consistency between public kindness and private kindness. Look for curiosity about your family, work, and limits.
Chemistry without safety is a headline, not a home. If you feel calm more often than you feel audited, you are probably with someone who can build.
Keep a private note of what felt good after dates. Memory favours drama. A written green flag is easier to trust when anxiety gets loud.

title: Love Languages That Actually Land in Real Life
excerpt: Words, time, help, touch, and gifts — translated for busy Indian couples.
author: Ishita Banerjee
content: The popular love-language idea is simple: people feel cared for in different currencies. One partner hears love in ‘I am proud of you’. Another feels it when you book the cab, call their mother, or sit down without a phone.

Guessing creates resentment. Ask, ‘What makes you feel chosen on a normal Tuesday?’ Then offer that thing in a size you can repeat. A daily two-minute check-in beats a rare expensive gesture that still misses.

Mismatch is normal. If you show love by fixing and they need listening, pause the solution for five minutes. If they buy gifts and you need time, name the evening you want before you criticise the present.
Languages change under stress. During exams, a new city, or a family wedding, ask again. MyTalk sessions are useful when you know you love each other and still feel unseen.

title: When Your Partner Pulls Away: Understanding Avoidant Distance
excerpt: Space is not always a breakup. Here is how to tell the difference and what to say.
author: Arjun Singh
content: An avoidant partner often cares and still needs air when emotions rise. Closeness can feel like pressure, so they go quiet, get busy, or change the subject. Chasing harder usually confirms their fear that love will swallow them.
Say the need without a verdict. ‘I miss you and I can give you tonight. Can we talk tomorrow at 8?’ A time boundary keeps space from becoming disappearance.
Watch behaviour over weeks, not one bad evening. Consistent return, repair, and honesty are green lights. Repeated vanishing with no plan is not a style. It is neglect.
You can love someone and still refuse a relationship where you do all the reaching. If you need a place to sort hurt from panic, a MyTalk listener can sit with you before you send the long message.

title: Anxious Attachment and Texting: How to Stop the Double-Text Spiral
excerpt: A practical way to sit with silence without sending five follow-up messages.
author: Meera Sharma
content: If a delayed reply feels like rejection, your nervous system is doing an old job: scan for abandonment. The phone makes that job louder. Seen receipts, typing bubbles, and last-seen stamps were never designed for anxious hearts.

Before you send the second message, ask what you want: information, comfort, or control. If it is comfort, texting them again rarely gives it. Put the phone in another room for twenty minutes, drink water, and write the fear in one sentence.
When you do write, keep it specific. ‘I felt dropped when plans stayed vague. Can we confirm Thursday?’ lands better than ‘Are you mad?’ or a joke that hides panic.
If texting anxiety is running your evenings, talk it through with someone who is not the person you are dating. MyTalk is built for that kind of private, low-pressure conversation.

title: Attachment Styles in Indian Relationships: Anxious, Avoidant, and Secure
excerpt: Why some people chase reassurance and others go quiet — and how family habits shape adult love.
author: MyTalk Editorial
content: Attachment style is the pattern you learned for closeness: reach, retreat, or stay steady. In many Indian homes, love was shown through food, fees, and duty more than through naming feelings, so adults often arrive at romance fluent in caretaking and clumsy with vulnerability.

Anxious attachment sounds like checking if they are online, replaying a short reply, and needing proof you matter. Avoidant attachment sounds like ‘I am fine’, delayed replies, and discomfort when a partner wants a plan. Secure attachment can ask, wait, and repair without making love a test.

You are not stuck with the style you inherited. Name the pattern out loud, slow the text spiral, and practise one clear request instead of a hint. A private MyTalk conversation can help you sort family loyalty from the bond you actually want.
Search this if you keep thinking ‘why am I like this in relationships’. The answer is usually history, not a character flaw.
